Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) distributes parameter shards across ranks, and when those ranks operate at different quantization precisions — say, BF16 for attention layers but INT8 for FFN blocks at tensor-parallel shard boundaries — gradient accumulation across micro-batches becomes a precision-mixing minefield: dequantization errors compound asymmetrically across shards before the all-reduce, meaning the aggregated gradient is not merely noisy but systematically biased in directions that depend on shard assignment rather than true loss curvature. The central question is: under what micro-batch heterogeneity conditions (varying sequence length, token distribution skew, or activation magnitude range) does this precision-boundary-induced bias exceed the signal threshold such that parameter updates diverge from the homogeneous-precision trajectory in ways that are not self-correcting? A beginner sees quantization error as uniform small noise and assumes it averages out across enough micro-batches; an expert knows that heterogeneous micro-batches create correlated quantization error — batches with high-magnitude activations hitting INT8 saturation will systematically underestimate gradients for those shards, and because FSDP's flat-parameter reconstruction happens post-reduce, there is no opportunity to reweight by precision tier before the update lands. The additional expert concern is shard-rank coupling: tensor parallelism means a single logical weight matrix is split across ranks, so a precision boundary mid-tensor means that row-wise gradient contributions from BF16 and INT8 sub-shards are summed as if they were commensurable, when in fact they carry different effective signal-to-noise ratios — the all-reduce silently launders this incommensurability into the final gradient. Variance explosion is the failure mode when high-magnitude outlier micro-batches drive INT8-quantized shard gradients into saturation repeatedly, producing gradient estimates that are both high-variance and low-fidelity, destabilizing Adam's second-moment estimator in ways that manifest as sudden loss spikes rather than gradual divergence.

FSDP's all-reduce operates on flattened gradient buffers — each rank contributes a contiguous block of fp32 (or bf16) values that represent its local gradient accumulation over the micro-batch sequence, and the collective averages these element-wise across ranks, producing a single gradient tensor that is then scattered back so each rank owns the update for its parameter shard. The critical structural fact is that this average is an unweighted mean of point estimates, not a weighted combination that accounts for the estimator quality of each contributing rank — a BF16 shard and an INT8 shard contribute with equal weight regardless of their gradient fidelity. INT8 saturation bias is non-canceling because it is conditionally dependent on activation magnitude, which is itself correlated across micro-batches through the data distribution: if your training corpus has domain clusters (long-form code vs. short social text), consecutive micro-batches within a cluster share similar activation magnitude profiles, meaning the bias hits the same shard directions repeatedly in the same sign, accumulating rather than averaging out. This is precisely the Jensen's inequality problem in quantization: E[Q(g)] ≠ Q(E[g]) when Q is a saturating function, and the expectation of the clipped gradient is strictly smaller in magnitude than the true gradient expectation for heavy-tailed gradient distributions — a property documented empirically in Dettmers et al.'s LLM.int8() work, where they observed systematic underestimation for weight rows with outlier activation channels. Under tensor parallelism the situation worsens because the all-reduce for a single weight matrix aggregates gradients from ranks that may have different quantization scales (per-shard dynamic range calibration), so what looks like a single averaged gradient is actually a sum of values calibrated to incommensurable scales — the rank with a tighter INT8 scale contributes a numerically smaller value that the optimizer interprets as a weaker gradient signal, not a less-reliable one. Adam's second-moment estimator then fits its adaptive learning rate to this distorted signal: it sees reduced variance on INT8-saturated shards (clipping compresses the distribution), which paradoxically increases the effective learning rate precisely for the parameters whose gradient estimates are least trustworthy.

Casting to fp32 before the all-reduce is a precision-preservation fix, not a bias-correction fix — it ensures no additional rounding error is introduced during the collective, but it does nothing about the fact that the gradient values arriving from INT8 shards are already systematically clipped; you are averaging fp32 representations of biased estimates, which produces a biased average with full fp32 fidelity. A principled fix at the communication layer requires metadata-augmented collectives: each rank must broadcast not just its gradient buffer but also its effective quantization scale and saturation mask (a bitmask indicating which gradient elements hit the INT8 clipping boundary), so the receiving side can perform a weighted reduce that downweights or corrects saturated contributions before averaging. The most rigorous version of this is a bias-corrected all-reduce analogous to Karimireddy et al.'s DIANA and later EF-SIGNSGD work on compressed gradient communication — the key insight from that line of research is that error feedback (accumulating the compression residual locally and adding it to the next round's gradient) transforms a biased compressor into an asymptotically unbiased one, and the same mechanism can be adapted to quantization-saturated shards by maintaining a per-shard error buffer that carries forward the clipped residual. Microsoft's ZeRO++ (2023) gestures toward this with its hierarchical quantization scheme (hq-ZeRO), which uses block-wise quantization with explicit scale factors transmitted alongside compressed gradients, but it does not address the saturation-bias problem specifically — it assumes the quantization error is symmetric and zero-mean, which breaks under activation outliers. A cleaner systems-level approach would be precision-aware reduce scatter: before the collective, ranks with INT8 boundaries flag their gradient contributions as low-fidelity, and the allreduce kernel applies a harmonic-mean weighting by inverse-variance of the gradient estimator rather than arithmetic-mean — this is implementable in NCCL custom reduction operators but requires exposing per-element reliability metadata that current FSDP implementations (PyTorch 2.x) do not track. The deepest obstacle to any such fix is that FSDP's flat-parameter design deliberately erases the correspondence between gradient buffer positions and the original tensor structure, making it architecturally difficult to recover which buffer elements correspond to INT8 vs. BF16 shards without invasive changes to the flattening and padding logic.
